cim_eredeti: Cybersecurity Month: AI, Deepfakes, and Digital Trust
szoveg_eredeti:
Learning how to verify information, assess digital trust, and use AI responsibly are rapidly becoming foundational skills for academic and professional success.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming higher education, health care, research, and the workplace. From helping students organize their studies to assisting researchers with data analysis and enabling professionals to work more efficiently, AI-powered tools are becoming part of everyday life.

At the same time, the same technologies that make AI useful can also be used by cybercriminals and fraudsters.

Artificial intelligence has dramatically lowered the barrier to creating convincing emails, realistic images, synthetic voices, and even video content that can be difficult to distinguish from reality. As a result, one of the most important cybersecurity skills today is no longer simply protecting devices or accounts. It is learning how to evaluate information and verify authenticity before acting.

For students, faculty, and staff, understanding the opportunities and risks associated with AI is becoming an essential part of digital literacy.

AI Is Changing the Cybersecurity Landscape

For years, cybercriminals often relied on poorly written phishing emails filled with spelling mistakes, suspicious language, and obvious warning signs.

Artificial intelligence has changed that.

A phishing email that once might have been easy to recognize can now appear polished and convincing.

AI allows attackers to create customized scams on a scale that was previously impossible. Instead of sending the same generic message to thousands of recipients, they can quickly generate unique messages tailored to specific individuals, departments, professions, or interests.

This means that cybersecurity increasingly depends on critical thinking rather than simply spotting spelling errors or poor formatting.

One of the most talked-about developments in AI is the rise of deepfakes. A deepfake is digital content, such as an image, audio recording, or video, that has been artificially generated or manipulated to appear authentic.

Deepfake technology can create realistic content depicting someone saying or doing something that never actually occurred.

In some cases, these synthetic creations are used for entertainment, education, accessibility, or creative purposes. However, they can also be used maliciously.

As AI tools become more powerful and more accessible, convincing synthetic content is becoming easier and less expensive to create.

Perhaps one of the most concerning developments is AI-generated voice cloning. With only a short sample of someone's voice, modern AI systems can create synthetic speech that closely resembles the original speaker.

Attackers have already begun using these capabilities to support fraud schemes.

Imagine receiving a voicemail that sounds exactly like:

The voice sounds familiar. The request seems reasonable. The message feels authentic.

Unfortunately, appearances can be deceiving.

The increasing realism of AI-generated voices means that people should be cautious about relying solely on the sound of a voice to verify identity, particularly when sensitive information, financial transactions, or account access are involved.

Universities are built on communication, collaboration, and trust.

Every day, people across campus receive messages regarding:

Cybercriminals understand this environment and frequently target institutions of higher education. A realistic AI-generated email might appear to come from a department administrator. A phone call may sound like a supervisor requesting urgent action. A manipulated image could be used to support a fraudulent request. These scenarios are becoming increasingly plausible.

For this reason, verification practices that once seemed excessive are quickly becoming standard cybersecurity safeguards.

One of the most important lessons in the AI era is that seeing is no longer believing. Historically, people relied heavily on visual evidence to establish trust. If a video showed someone speaking, many assumed the content was genuine. If a voice sounded familiar, most people accepted its authenticity.

Today, those assumptions are no longer always reliable. Instead, individuals should develop the habit of independently verifying unusual requests.

Verification may feel inconvenient, but it remains one of the most effective defenses against both traditional and AI-enabled scams.

Although deepfakes are improving rapidly, many still contain clues that something is not quite right.

Scammers often pressure victims to act immediately. Be cautious when someone insists that there is no time to verify a request.

Unexpected requests involving these items deserve additional scrutiny.

Communication That Feels Out of Character

Even when content appears convincing, pay attention to context.

Often, the surrounding circumstances provide better indicators than the content itself.

It is important to remember that artificial intelligence itself is not the problem. In fact, AI is helping defenders improve cybersecurity in many ways.

Many of the same technologies used by attackers are also being deployed to strengthen defenses.

The goal is not to fear AI but to understand both its benefits and its limitations. Like any powerful technology, responsible use is essential.

The most effective defense against misinformation, scams, and deepfakes is not a particular software product. It is an informed and skeptical user.

Digital resilience means developing habits that help you navigate an environment where information may not always be what it appears to be.

The ability to evaluate information critically has become just as important as the ability to secure a password or recognize a phishing email.

Artificial intelligence will continue to evolve and become more deeply integrated into society. Students will encounter it in classrooms and future careers. Researchers will leverage it to accelerate discovery. Faculty and staff will use it to improve productivity and streamline administrative work.

The future will bring tremendous opportunities, but it will also require new forms of awareness and responsibility.

Learning how to verify information, assess digital trust, and use AI responsibly are rapidly becoming foundational skills for academic and professional success.

Artificial intelligence is changing how we learn, work, communicate, and create. It is also changing how cybercriminals attempt to deceive people.

As deepfakes, voice cloning, and AI-generated content become more sophisticated, trust can no longer be based solely on what we see or hear.

The most valuable cybersecurity skill in the AI era is verification. By slowing down, confirming unusual requests, and maintaining healthy skepticism, every member of the campus community can help protect themselves and others from emerging threats.

In a world where anything can be generated, verification becomes the foundation of trust.
